trainers.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions about Brooke’s experiment.

atoms.text: Brooke wants to test how surface area affects friction. She decides that she will pull some items from her kitchen across a table and measure which is the hardest to pull.

atoms.a: Should she pull each item across the same or different surfaces?

feedback.correct: By keeping as many details of the experiment the same as possible, Brooke’s experiment will remain fair.
feedback.wrong: Not quite. Depending on the roughness of each surface, different amounts of friction would be produced, and the reliability of Brooke’s results would be affected.

atoms.a: What should Brooke use to measure how difficult it is to pull each item?

feedback.end: By using a forcemeter, Brooke’s measurements will not only be accurate, but also numerical — making them easier to compare.

atoms.a: Aside from the surface area of each item’s base, what other factor could affect the friction produced?
What could Brooke do to fix this problem?

instruction.text: Fill in the gaps in Brooke’s hypothesis.

atoms.sound: I think the larger the base of the item, the more friction will be produced.

instruction.text: Brooke pulls each of the items using the forcemeter. Record the values for each item in the table below.

trainers.layout:
a1 b1
a2 b2
a3 b3
a4 b4

hint.label: Newtons (N)
hint.text: N represents newtons: the unit used to measure force.

trainers.instruction: Which item produced the most friction?
trainers.hint: The higher the force needed to pull the item, the more friction produced.

trainers.instruction: Which item’s base has the smallest surface area?
trainers.hint: The less friction produced, the smaller the surface area in contact with the table.

instruction.text: Fill in the gaps in Brooke’s conclusion.

atoms.b: In the experiment, the ((++results ideas)) proved that larger surface areas produce more ((++friction water)).
